memo:
I have decided to cover the $112.1 million shortfall mainly from customers, the workforce and shareholders, while protecting the Company's future and the environment.

Prices: $30.0 million from a list-price increase of about 2.4%, below the 3.5% that the sales organization says customers would accept without losing volume. This leaves a margin of safety in case the downturn makes customers more price-sensitive.

Suppliers: $7.7 million, the full negotiated saving on the 30% of supplier spending up for renewal, at a 4% price reduction on the lower volume.

Workforce: $40.0 million from eliminating roles, weighted toward management and business and financial operations, where pay per role is highest and the reduction does the most good per role lost. Severance will be paid from cash in addition to this. $10.0 million from a wage and hours reduction, about 4.5% of the remaining payroll, well inside the 10% limit even after the role cuts.

Shareholders: $24.4 million of lower operating income. This is the direct cost to owners and it is the part I would most like to avoid, but it is needed to close the gap without damaging the business.

Protected: R&D is left at its full $30.0 million because it funds the product updates and controls software that drive future revenue, and cutting it would weaken the Company's position when the cycle turns. Environmental projects are left at $4.5 million; these are energy and emissions upgrades that also reduce operating costs over time.

Payouts are not part of this decision and are set separately by the board. Given the lower earnings, the board may wish to review the $146.1 million paid to shareholders against the coming year's reduced net income, and I would recommend it do so.

The plan leaves the Company's liquidity intact, with $44.1 million of cash above the minimum and a $300.0 million undrawn facility available if the downturn runs longer than expected.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall so that customers, suppliers and shareholders carry most of it, and the workforce carries a bounded share, while protecting future products.

Customers bear the full $44.6 million price increase, the maximum customers would accept on the lower revenue. Suppliers bear the full $7.7 million saving from renegotiating agreements. Environmental projects give $4.5 million, the full discretionary budget; permit-required compliance spending is untouched. I have not cut research and development: it funds the product updates and controls software that will matter when demand recovers, and its engineering payroll is a long-term asset.

The workforce bears $42.0 million. I propose eliminating $30.0 million of roles, drawn mainly from salaried and non-plant functions such as management, business operations and administration, where the payroll is largest relative to plant output. This brings a one-time severance cost, which I estimate at roughly $3 to $4 million, paid from cash on hand of $144.9 million and the undrawn $300 million facility. I also propose a $12.0 million reduction in wages or hours, about 5% of the remaining payroll, below the 10% ceiling. It is applied to the reduced payroll after eliminations, lowering its ceiling by 7.9% of the eliminated amount, so I have kept it well inside the limit.

Shareholders bear the residual $13.3 million through lower operating income. I have left dividends and repurchases to the board, as they do not affect operating income.

The plan keeps the plants and their skilled staff largely intact, protects product development, and keeps leverage manageable at debt of about 2.3 times EBITDA before the downturn's effect. It is a balanced response that preserves value over the next four quarters.

Decision: close the $112.1M shortfall with the cheapest lines that keep the Company's earning power intact, avoiding a direct hit to shareholders' operating income.

Prices ($44.6M): the full increase customers would accept (3.5%) is taken. It is the highest-value lever because it adds to margin without cutting cost, though it carries some risk of lost volume in a downturn; we will monitor order intake closely.

Suppliers ($7.7M): the full negotiating limit is taken on contracts coming up for renewal. Suppliers bear this through lower prices; we accept the relationship risk and will keep payment terms fair.

Environmental projects ($4.5M): the discretionary budget is cut in full. Permit-required compliance spending ($3.0M) is untouched. This is the least value-destructive cut available, but it does fall on communities and the environment, and we will restore it when volumes recover.

Role eliminations ($55.3M of payroll and benefits): this is the balance. Eliminating roles removes about $1.27 of annual cost per dollar of payroll, far more efficiently than a wage cut, which would also be capped and shrink with each role removed. Severance is a one-time cash cost, which we fund from cash above the minimum operating level. Roles will be drawn from functions where the Company has the most depth and the least direct effect on plant output, prioritizing management and salaried positions, and we will avoid cuts to the plants' core production and maintenance capacity.

Not used: R&D is protected because it funds the products and software that drive recovery. Wage and hours cuts are not needed. Accepting lower operating income would put the full $112.1M on shareholders at a cost of roughly $0.79 of net income per dollar, so it is the most costly option and is avoided.

Dividends and repurchases are a separate board decision and are not changed here.

Decision on the $112.1 million shortfall, allocated to protect the Company's long-term earning power while sharing the burden fairly.

Prices ($44.6M): We take the full 3.5% increase the sales organization believes customers will accept without losing volume. This is the largest single lever and keeps the cost of the downturn off shareholders. It carries real risk in a downturn, and we will monitor order rates closely after the price change.

Suppliers ($7.7M): We take the full available saving on the 30% of spend renewing next year, applied to the lower volume base.

Environmental projects ($4.5M): We cut the discretionary project budget in full. Permitted compliance spending of $3.0M is untouched. This is a modest cut, and we will look to restore the projects as volumes recover.

Research and development ($0): We protect R&D. It funds the product updates and controls software that customers buy, and cutting it would weaken the Company's position when the cycle turns.

Roles and wages ($33.55M in roles, $21.75M in wages and hours): We eliminate roles and reduce wages and hours, and we keep the total cut to the minimum needed. Because roles eliminated reduce the wage-cut ceiling, we solved the two together. Severance on eliminated roles will be paid from cash, which the balance sheet can absorb. Priority for role reductions should go to management and non-plant positions where possible, and wage or hour reductions should be spread across the remaining payroll.

Shareholders: we accept no reduction in operating income beyond what these levers deliver, so the $112.1M is fully covered without a profit cut. Dividend and repurchase decisions remain with the board and are not part of this allocation.

The coming-year shortfall is $112.1 million, from a 15% fall in revenue. I have chosen to protect shareholder value by absorbing as little of it as possible through lower operating income, and spreading it across the lines that cost the least to the Company's long-term earning power.

Price: I am taking the full $44.6 million increase available on the lower revenue. The sales organization estimates customers will accept 3.5% without losing volume, so this carries little volume risk. Suppliers: the full $7.7 million from renegotiating renewing agreements, which covers the 30% of spend up for renewal. Environmental projects: the full $4.5 million discretionary budget. Compliance spending is required by permit and is untouched. R&D: no cut. Cutting it would weaken the product pipeline and the engineering base that drives future revenue, which costs more shareholder value over four quarters than the saving gains.

Roles and wages: $45.0 million of roles eliminated, drawn mainly from management, business and financial operations, and office support where the work can be consolidated. Severance of roughly $5 million is paid once from cash, which is covered by the $44.1 million of cash above minimum and the undrawn $300 million facility. I am also taking $10.3 million from wage and hour reductions on the remaining payroll, within the reduced limit after the eliminated roles. Production and maintenance pay is largely protected to preserve plant capacity and the hiring pipeline.

Lower operating income: none. Accepting a profit reduction would fall directly on shareholders. Dividends and repurchases are set separately and are not part of this decision.

The result is that shareholders bear no operating-income loss, but the workforce bears the cost through roles and pay, and customers and suppliers contribute through price and terms. The board should expect severance costs and a restructuring of the management layer, and should monitor the effect on plant execution during the downturn.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall to the sources that protect long-term shareholder value and avoid harming the Company's future.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving. This is 4.0% on the 30% of spend renewing next year and is a normal result of negotiation.

Customers bear $44.6 million through a 3.5% price increase. The sales organization judges this acceptable without loss of unit volume, and it matches the increase we took in the year just ended. Because the downturn is volume-driven, I am relying on that estimate; if volume falls further, this line is the one to revisit first.

The workforce bears $59.8 million through eliminated roles, measured at payroll and benefits together. I have concentrated these reductions in management and back-office functions, where payroll is largest relative to plant operations, rather than in production, where we need people for the 1,900 plant and field-service roles. Severance of roughly 8.3% to 12.4% of pay will be paid from cash in the coming year; I have not counted it in the savings figure, and it should be budgeted separately.

I have not cut research and development, because it funds the products and controls that will matter when volumes recover. I have not cut wages or hours, because it would fall on the whole workforce and damage morale and retention. I have not cut environmental projects, because the budget is small and the reduction would fall on communities near the plants. I have not accepted lower operating income, so shareholders do not bear the decline directly, though they do bear the severance cost and the reduced capacity.

The Company's cash remains above its minimum operating level, and the undrawn facility provides a buffer against timing differences in the severance payments.

We must absorb a $112.1 million operating income shortfall from a 15% volume decline. I have spread the burden so that the people and programs that build future value are protected, while shareholders carry the residual.

Customers bear $44.6 million through a 3.5% list-price increase, the maximum the sales organization believes customers will accept without losing volume. This is the largest and most reliable lever, and it aligns with the last year's pricing.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through renegotiating the 30% of spend coming up for renewal. This is a 4% reduction on those contracts, at the limit of what purchasing thinks obtainable.

The workforce bears $40.0 million through eliminating roles, weighted toward management, business and financial operations, and office support rather than plant production. Much of this can come through attrition and by not backfilling the roles that fall vacant, which avoids most severance. Severance is paid from cash, and the Company has about $44 million of cash above its minimum, so this must be managed carefully. Plant staff are largely retained, since the plants hired 500 people last year and will need skills during recovery.

I have not cut wages or hours. A pay cut would reduce the maximum available from roles and would damage retention and morale at the moment we most need experienced people.

I have not cut R&D or environmental projects. R&D funds the product pipeline and controls software that position the Company for recovery. Environmental projects are a small saving that would not justify the reputational and community cost.

Shareholders bear the remaining $19.8 million as lower operating income. Payouts are a separate board decision and are not changed here. The board should review the dividend and repurchase level against the reduced earnings and the cash position, as the current payout is 90% of last year's net income.

We are covering the $112.1 million shortfall with a mix that protects the Company's ability to recover when the downturn ends.

Prices: we take the full $44.6 million available from the largest list-price increase customers would accept (3.5%). The sales organization's estimate supports this without a volume loss, and it is the cheapest source of recovery.

Suppliers: we take the full $7.7 million from renegotiating the 30% of spending coming up for renewal, using the 4.0% reduction purchasing considers obtainable.

Roles: we eliminate $30.0 million of payroll and benefits, concentrated in non-plant functions such as management, office support and business operations, where losing a role is least likely to affect output. This costs one-time severance paid from cash, which we accept. We avoid production, maintenance and field-service roles: they took 500 hires last year, cost $15,000 each to retrain, and take six months to become productive, so cutting them now would be expensive to reverse.

Wages and hours: we cut $15.0 million, well under the cap after the role eliminations, spread across remaining payroll, to limit the morale and retention effect.

Shareholders: we accept $14.8 million lower operating income, the smallest share, because it falls directly on shareholders.

Protected lines: we do not cut R&D, because it funds the products that will drive value after the downturn, and we do not cut environmental projects, because the saving is small and the reputational and community cost is not worth it.

Net effect: the shortfall is absorbed across customers, suppliers, the workforce and shareholders, with no cut to future products or to the plants' ability to meet demand when orders return. Payouts are unchanged here; the board may revisit them separately given the lower cash generation expected.

The $112.1 million shortfall is split across five sources, chosen to protect the Company's long-term value while being honest about what shareholders absorb.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving. Supplier renewals are a normal commercial lever and the cost is spread across many counterparties.

The workforce bears $65.0 million: $50.0 million of role eliminations (about $63.4 million of payroll and benefits, concentrated in non-core roles and attrition where possible, with severance paid from cash) and a $15.0 million wage and hours reduction. The wage cut is below its cap of about $20.5 million, which falls as roles are eliminated, and is applied to remaining payroll, so it is a moderate and temporary measure rather than a pay cut across the board.

Shareholders bear $39.4 million of lower operating income. I am not raising prices, since customers are cutting orders and a price rise would likely cost volume and deepen the downturn. I am not cutting R&D or environmental projects: R&D funds the products and controls that will drive recovery, and the environmental projects protect the communities near the plants and the permitted operations. These cuts would create short-term savings at the expense of value the Company needs after the downturn.

The main risk is cash. Operating income falls to about $126 million and EBITDA to roughly $179 million, which raises debt to EBITDA well above 2.3 times. The board should review the payout level against this lower earnings base and the $300 million undrawn facility, which provides a backstop. I recommend monitoring plant 6, which already loses money, for consolidation options.

The downturn cuts operating income by $112.1 million. I have spread the shortfall across the parties while protecting the Company's future and its communities.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving from renegotiating renewing agreements. This is the least-damaging lever, since it falls on supplier margins rather than on our own capacity.

Customers bear $20.0 million through a price increase of roughly 2% rather than the 3.5% the sales team says customers would accept. I am deliberately using less than the ceiling: in a downturn, pushing price to the limit risks losing unit volume, which would cost more than it saves.

The workforce bears $62.0 million. I plan to eliminate roles worth $47.0 million in payroll and benefits, concentrated in management and non-plant functions, where the Company can absorb the change, and to cut wages or hours by $15.0 million on the remaining payroll. Plant production and maintenance staff are largely protected, because we need that capacity to recover when orders return, and we will fill some needs through redeployment instead of new hiring. Severance is a one-time cash cost to be funded from cash above the minimum and the undrawn facility.

I am not cutting R&D or environmental projects. Those budgets protect the products and reputation that drive value over the coming years, and their savings are small relative to the risk.

Shareholders bear the remaining $22.4 million as lower operating income. This is the price of keeping the organization intact through a cyclical downturn. Payout decisions are outside this decision and remain with the board, which should review them against the lower earnings outlook.

The coming year's revenue falls $225.0 million on lower volume, cutting operating income by $112.1 million to $126.4 million. I have allocated that shortfall across the stakeholders who can absorb it most sensibly, and kept shareholders' share to the remainder.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full purchasing estimate on the contracts up for renewal. Customers bear $44.6 million through a list-price increase of 3.5%, the largest increase the sales organization believes they will accept without losing volume. Higher prices are the least costly lever, but I have not pushed beyond that estimate because volume loss would cost more than it gains.

The workforce bears $20.0 million through eliminating roles, concentrated in management, business and financial operations, and office support, to be achieved mainly through attrition and consolidation rather than plant layoffs. This is sized well below the $309.8 million ceiling. Severance of roughly $2 million will be paid from cash, which remains comfortably above the minimum operating level. I have made no cut to wages or hours, to protect morale and the plants during a downturn in which we will need to recover volume.

The environment bears $2.0 million, a partial cut to discretionary energy-efficiency and emissions projects. Compliance spending is untouched. R&D is protected in full, because engineering capability and new models are what will drive the recovery.

Shareholders bear the remaining $37.8 million through lower operating income. This is the honest allocation: owners carry the residual risk of a downturn. Dividends and repurchases are outside this decision and are not changed here. Debt to EBITDA will rise somewhat, but leverage remains manageable and the revolver is undrawn.

The package protects the franchise, keeps plants and engineering intact, and spreads the cost fairly, while keeping shareholders' exposure to a level the business can carry.

The downturn removes $112.1 million of operating income. I have spread it across the lines that protect the franchise best, and I have kept the cuts to future capability and the environment at zero.

Supplier savings of $7.7 million are the full amount available. They are low-risk and fall on suppliers rather than on our people or customers.

Price increases of $30.0 million are well below the 3.5% ceiling ($44.6 million). Customers are under pressure in a downturn, and we need volume to recover, so I have not pushed price to the limit.

Eliminating roles of $55.0 million is the main lever. It is weighted toward non-plant functions and toward roles that fall with lower production volume, and it avoids cutting the engineering and maintenance capacity that protects the installed base and the parts and service business, which is 25% of revenue and has the steadiest margin. Severance is a one-off cash cost that the board should expect. Redeploying staff rather than hiring from outside will reduce future recruiting cost.

A wage and hours reduction of $8.0 million is applied to the payroll that remains after role cuts, within the reduced cap. It is kept modest because it falls on the workforce.

R&D, at zero, and environmental projects, at zero, are protected. Cutting R&D would damage future products; cutting environmental projects would fall on communities near the plants and on our permit standing.

The residual $11.4 million falls on shareholders as lower operating income. This is the cost of protecting people, products and the environment. Dividends and repurchases are a separate board decision, and the board should review them given the lower earnings, since current payouts equal 90% of last year's net income.

The $112.1 million shortfall is spread across six sources, with research and development left intact because it protects future products and the engineering staff who build them, the Company's main source of long-term value.

Customers bear $44.6 million through a price increase, the full amount on the reduced revenue base and close to the sales organization's estimate of the largest increase customers would accept without losing volume. This is the most efficient source, but it carries some risk of lost orders in a downturn, so the board should watch unit volume closely.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through lower prices on contracts coming up for renewal. Environmental projects bear $4.5 million, the full discretionary budget. Permit-required compliance spending is untouched.

The workforce bears $46.0 million: $40.0 million from eliminating roles (payroll and benefits, with severance paid from cash, not counted here) and $6.0 million from a wage and hours reduction on the payroll that remains. The wage cut is well inside its cap of about $21.2 million after the role reductions. The role reductions are the largest single cost to people, and I recommend that they be made through attrition and by function where possible, and that the plants' staffing be reviewed for the loss-making Plant 6.

Shareholders bear $9.3 million as lower operating income. I have chosen to take this rather than cut further into people or future products, since it is the smallest amount that closes the gap.

Payouts are not part of this decision and are left to the board. Severance costs and the cash effect of the role reductions should be reflected in the coming year's cash plan, which has room above the minimum operating level and the undrawn facility as a backstop.

The downturn removes $112.1 million of operating income. I have spread that shortfall across the lines that do the least lasting harm to the franchise and that are most recoverable, and kept a meaningful share on shareholders rather than pushing everything onto the workforce.

Customers bear the largest share, $44.6 million, through the full 3.5% list-price increase the sales organization believes customers will accept. This is a risk in a downturn, but it is the cleanest source and does not cost jobs.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving on renewals. Environmental projects are cut in full, $4.5 million; compliance spending required by permits is untouched. Environmental cuts are discretionary and temporary, and I will flag the reduction to the board.

The workforce bears $45.0 million: $30.0 million from eliminating roles, which carries one-time severance paid from cash and is the most durable saving, and $15.0 million from a wage and hour reduction applied to the remaining payroll. This is within the reduced cap of about $22.0 million after the role reductions. I have prioritised attrition and redeployment where possible, since plants hired 500 people last year and some of those roles can absorb staff from other functions.

I am not cutting research and development. It protects the new models and controls software that will matter when volumes recover, and cutting it would damage the Company's future value. Shareholders bear the residual $10.3 million as lower operating income. Payouts are set separately by the board and are not part of this decision.

Net, this keeps the Company's competitive position and engineering capacity intact while limiting the cash drain of the downturn. I will monitor price realisation, which is the largest single assumption, and revisit the mix quarterly.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall across six sources so that the cost falls mainly where it does the least lasting damage to shareholder value. I have not cut research and development ($0). The $30 million budget funds the product updates and controls software that keep the Company competitive when orders recover, and cutting it would trade a temporary downturn for a permanent loss of position. Engineering pay is also protected for the same reason.

Eliminating roles bears $35.0 million, concentrated in management and administrative functions, where the payroll pool is largest relative to the work lost. I avoided plant roles: the Company hired 500 production, maintenance and warehouse people last year, and replacing them costs about $15,000 each plus six months of reduced output. Severance on this reduction is a one-time cash cost that I accept.

A wage and hours reduction of $15.0 million, well inside the cap on the remaining payroll, is applied across the workforce. Price increases of $30.0 million are set below the 3.5% ceiling of $44.6 million, because pushing customers harder in a downturn risks volume that would cost more than it gains. Supplier savings of $7.7 million, the full available amount, and environmental projects of $4.5 million, the full discretionary budget, are both taken; compliance spending is untouched.

The remaining $19.9 million is accepted as lower operating income, borne by shareholders. This is the honest cost of the downturn and it is the smallest sacrifice that leaves the workforce and the product pipeline intact. Dividends and repurchases are not part of this decision and are left to the board, though the board should weigh that the current payout of 90% of net income is high relative to a shrinking earnings base.

The coming-year shortfall is $112.1M on a 15% revenue fall. I have spread it across all parties instead of loading it onto one.

Suppliers bear $7.7M, the full negotiated saving available on the lower volume. This is the cheapest source: it comes from renewals and does not touch our workforce or customers.

The environment and nearby communities bear $4.5M, the full discretionary environmental projects budget. Permitted compliance spending of $3.0M is untouched, so no regulatory obligation is at risk.

Customers bear $30.0M through a 2.4% list-price increase, below the 3.5% ceiling of $44.6M. Pushing to the ceiling in a downturn risks unit volume, which would undo the gain.

The workforce bears $60.0M: $50.0M through eliminating roles, weighted toward management and business and financial operations, with attrition used where possible, and $10.0M through a modest wage or hours reduction, well inside the 10% cap. I have kept the cut below the ceiling deliberately. Severance is paid from cash, and we hired 500 plant workers last year at real cost, so I prefer to keep the skilled production and maintenance base intact for recovery.

Shareholders bear $9.9M through lower operating income. I have not cut R&D: the $30.0M funds the product and controls work that drives future revenue, and cutting it would trade long-term value for a short-term number.

Dividends and repurchases are the board's separate decision and are not part of this allocation. Because they now exceed net income, I recommend the board review them in light of the downturn.

The total is exactly $112.1M.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall so that the cost falls on the least valuable parts of the business and not on the future of the Company or its plant workforce.

Prices: I am taking the full $44.6 million available from a 3.5% list-price increase. This is the largest increase the sales organization believes customers will accept without losing volume, so it protects margin without the volume loss that would compound the downturn.

Suppliers: I am taking the full $7.7 million available from renegotiating the agreements up for renewal. This is the purchasing department's estimate of what is achievable on the lower volume.

Environmental projects: I am cutting the full $4.5 million of discretionary projects. Permitted compliance spending of $3.0 million is untouched. This cut has a real cost to the environment and nearby communities, and the board should be told that it is a temporary measure to be restored when volumes recover.

Eliminating roles: I am covering the remaining $55.3 million of payroll and benefits by eliminating roles outside the plants' production, maintenance and warehouse work, mainly in management, business and financial operations, and office support. This keeps the people who build, maintain and ship the machines in place. Severance will be paid from cash in addition to this figure.

Not used: I am not cutting research and development, which protects future products. I am not cutting wages or hours, which would fall on the plant workforce. I am not accepting lower operating income, which would fall directly on shareholders.

Dividends and repurchases are a separate board decision and are not changed here. The main risk is that the role eliminations are deeper than the business needs once volume recovers, so I recommend reviewing the management structure at the next quarter's close.

Decision: of the $112.1 million shortfall, $60.0 million is borne by the workforce through eliminating roles, $7.7 million by suppliers through renegotiated prices, and $44.4 million by shareholders as lower operating income.

Roles are the first lever because they are the largest recurring saving and I am concentrating them where they least affect production capacity: management, office and administrative support, business and financial operations, sales, and IT, with the remainder in production and warehouse roles tied to lower volume, including at Plant 6, which is loss-making. Severance of roughly 8 to 12 percent of annual pay will be paid from cash, reducing the near-term cash cushion, which is already limited to about $44 million above the minimum operating level. I am not cutting wages or hours: it would reduce retention and applies to a shrinking payroll, so its value is small relative to its cost.

I am not raising prices. Volume is already falling 15 percent; a price increase in a downturn risks further volume loss and would push cost onto customers who are themselves under pressure.

I am protecting R&D and environmental projects. R&D funds the products and controls that drive recovery, and cutting it would impair future value. Environmental projects are small and their cut would damage community relations at a time we need them.

Shareholders bear $44.4 million through lower earnings rather than through deeper workforce cuts. That is a real cost, and it means the current payout of $146.1 million exceeds earnings in the coming year. I recommend the board review dividends and repurchases in light of this, since payouts are outside this decision. Our debt-to-EBITDA ratio should be monitored as EBITDA falls.
